keyVerseText: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.
rootMeaning: The Greek noun ποιητής (poiētḗs) stems from the verb ποιέω (poiéō), which broadly means to make, do, or bring about. This root conveys the idea of one who actively produces or creates something. Beyond the English gloss of 'poet' or 'doer,' the root sense emphasizes agency and intentionality in bringing something into existence, whether it be a work, a law, or a creative composition.
usageInScripture: Across its six occurrences, ποιητής is primarily translated as 'a doer' three times, with other renderings including 'poets,' 'the doers,' and 'doers.' This range shows the term's flexibility, referring both to creators in the artistic sense and to those who act or perform deeds, especially in relation to the law or works. The consistent underlying theme is one of active participation and authorship, whether in speech, law, or creative arts.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ποιητής as both a maker and doer enriches our grasp of divine and human roles in Scripture. God is the ultimate ποιητής, the Creator and lawgiver, who brings all things into being and ordains order. Believers, called to be doers of the word, reflect this creative and active nature by living out God's commands. Recognizing this word's full semantic range helps us appreciate the dynamic relationship between God's sovereign creative work and our faithful response in action and obedience.
keyVerseReflection: In Acts 17:28, Paul quotes 'your own poets' to affirm that 'in him we live, and move, and have our being,' highlighting humanity's dependence on God as the source of life and existence. The use of ποιητής here underscores the role of poets as creators of meaningful expression who, even in their human artistry, point to the truth of God as the ultimate origin. This enriches the verse by connecting human creativity with divine creativity, reminding us that all life and movement are grounded in God, the supreme ποιητής.
